Scalar and strict-fluid instances are [[thm-gr-scalar-field-local-evolution]], [[thm-gr-barotropic-fluid-local-evolution]]. Geodesic nonnegative tilted dust instead uses [[thm-gr-dust-local-evolution]] with its independent common-flow/frame reduction, including its separately prescribed velocity on zero density. Complete data, including all required matter jets, agree by [L2]; the comparison isometry matches every matter field. An arbitrary conserved stress is not a fixed-model uniqueness premise.

steps.claim: (Local uniqueness on the whole restart surface.) The complete data of $S$ realized in $M$ and in $M'$ via $\Phi|_S$ agree by [L2]. Apply [L4] to obtain intrinsic Cauchy neighborhoods of each surface, carrying the restricted metric and full matter solution. The applicable fixed-model theorem [L3] gives an open neighborhood $O$ of the whole $S$ in the source and a future isometry $\Theta:O\to M'$ matching all matter fields, with $\Theta|_S=\Phi|_S$. Replace $O$ by $O\cap N$. This construction uses the actual branch uniqueness theorem and its admissibility at the realized restart data.

facts.label: L4
facts.text: [L4] The restart supplier makes $S$ a smooth embedded spacelike hypersurface without boundary. The intrinsic neighborhood theorem [[lem-gr-local-cauchy-neighborhood]] clause (d), applied separately to the embeddings $S\hookrightarrow M$ and $\Phi(S)\hookrightarrow M'$, supplies open neighborhoods on which the whole respective surface is Cauchy and which are globally hyperbolic. With the restricted solution fields these are developments of the complete data on $S$. Neither surface needs to be globally acausal in the original ambient manifold; the neighborhoods are intrinsic.

($U\cup N_0$ is a development.) By [L6] every causal curve in $U\cup N_0$ that is inextendible in $U\cup N_0$ meets $\Sigma$ in exactly one parameter value; $U\cup N_0\subseteq M$ is open with the restricted metric, time orientation and matter fields, the field equations hold (they are local and hold on $M$), and $j:\Sigma\to U\cup N_0$ is an embedding with the induced data $(h,K,\psi_0)$. Hence $U\cup N_0$ is a development of the same data ([[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a)); in particular it is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $\Sigma$ by [[thm-gr-cauchy-surface-implies-globally-hyperbolic]].

facts.label: L2
facts.text: [L2] Cauchy properties and the side decomposition: every causal curve in $U_i$ that is inextendible in $U_i$ meets $\Sigma$ in exactly one parameter value; $M=I^-(\Sigma)\sqcup\Sigma\sqcup I^+(\Sigma)$; and every closed causal segment lies on an inextendible causal curve of the ambient manifold, up to a strictly increasing affine reparametrization ([[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a), [[lem-gr-cauchy-set-topology-and-graph]] clause (a), [[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clause (c)).

steps.claim: (Setup.) Let $\gamma:I\to W$ be a future causal curve that is inextendible in $W$, and suppose for contradiction that $\gamma$ misses $\Sigma$. Then $\gamma$ is a causal curve in each $U_i$ and in $M$. Since $I$ is an interval and $\gamma$ is continuous, $\gamma(I)$ is connected; by [L2] it is contained in $I^+(\Sigma)$ or in $I^-(\Sigma)$. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ throughout if necessary (which exchanges $I^+$ and $I^-$, preserves every hypothesis and the property of being a development, and exchanges past and future), we may assume $\gamma(I)\subseteq I^+(\Sigma)$.

(Uniqueness of the meeting and conclusion.) Suppose $t_1<t_2$ in $I$ with $\gamma(t_1),\gamma(t_2)\in\Sigma$. By [L2] there is an inextendible causal curve $\hat\gamma:J\to M$ and a strictly increasing affine $\rho$ with $\hat\gamma\circ\rho=\gamma|_{[t_1,t_2]}$; since $\hat\gamma$ is a causal curve in the development $M$ with Cauchy surface $\Sigma$, it meets $\Sigma$ in at most one parameter value, but $\hat\gamma(\rho(t_1)),\hat\gamma(\rho(t_2))\in\Sigma$ with $\rho(t_1)<\rho(t_2)$, a contradiction. Hence the meeting is unique, and $\Sigma$ is a Cauchy set of the Lorentzian manifold $W$ in the sense of [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c) (past-directed curves are the time reverse of the argument). Moreover $W$ is an open submanifold of $M$ with the restricted Lorentzian metric, time orientation and matter fields; the field equations are local and hold on $M$, hence on $W$; and $j:\Sigma\to W$ is an embedding whose induced metric, second fundamental form and matter data are those of the data. Therefore $W$ is a development of the same data in the sense of [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a).

steps.claim: (A compact set containing the past part.) Fix $t_0\in I$. By [L3] the set $K:=J^+(\Sigma)\cap J^-(\gamma(t_0))$ is compact. (The original past tail converges.) For $s<t_0$ put $L(s)=\ell_h(\gamma|_{[s,t_0]})$, which is bounded above by $L(K)$ by [L3]. Write $L_*=\sup_{s<t_0}L(s)$. For $s<t<t_0$, integral additivity gives $\ell_h(\gamma|_{[s,t]})=L(s)-L(t)\le L_*-L(t)$, which tends to zero as $t$ approaches the past parameter end. The same bound shows the entire original past tail converges to $y$. Compactness of $K$ makes it closed, so $y\in K\subseteq J^+(\Sigma)$. This works at finite and infinite original parameter ends without reparametrization.

facts.text: [L4] The auxiliary metric $h$ of [[thm-gr-auxiliary-complete-riemannian-metric]] has a complete distance inducing the topology. Distance between two points of a compact subarc is at most its $h$-length. Thus finite total tail length makes image points Cauchy at that end, without changing the original parametrization ([[def-metric-convergence]], [[def-complete-metric-space]], [[def-continuity-real]]).

steps.claim: (The original past tail converges.) For $s<t_0$ put $L(s)=\ell_h(\gamma|_{[s,t_0]})$, which is bounded above by $L(K)$ by [L3]. Write $L_*=\sup_{s<t_0}L(s)$. For $s<t<t_0$, integral additivity gives $\ell_h(\gamma|_{[s,t]})=L(s)-L(t)\le L_*-L(t)$, which tends to zero as $t$ approaches the past parameter end. Choose a decreasing coinitial sequence in this real interval. Distance is bounded by these tail lengths, so its image points are Cauchy and converge to $y$ by [L4]. The same bound shows the entire original past tail converges to $y$. Compactness of $K$ makes it closed, so $y\in K\subseteq J^+(\Sigma)$. This works at finite and infinite original parameter ends without reparametrization.

facts.label: L3
facts.text: [L3] Convexity and the Cauchy property: causal curves in $M$ with endpoints in $U$ lie in $U$, and likewise for their time reverses; an inextendible causal curve in $M$ (respectively in $U$) meets $\Sigma$ (respectively $\Sigma$) in exactly one parameter value; Cauchy sets are acausal; and every closed causal segment lies on an inextendible causal curve of the ambient manifold ([[lem-gr-subdevelopment-convexity]] clause (c), [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a)5, [[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (c)-(d), [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]).

steps.claim: (The Cauchy property.) An inextendible causal curve in $Q$ has a maximal portion in any open member image that it meets. By [L4] that portion is inextendible in the member and hence meets its Cauchy surface, so the whole curve meets $\bar j(\Sigma)$ at least once. For uniqueness, the sets $Q^\pm=p_M(I_M^\pm(\Sigma))\cup p_{M'}(I_{M'}^\pm(\Sigma'))$ are open and disjoint, and $Q=Q^-\sqcup\bar j(\Sigma)\sqcup Q^+$: this follows from the member side decompositions and their agreement on the common subdevelopment by causal convexity and future cone preservation. The surface is closed since its trace in each open member image is the closed member Cauchy surface. Near any surface point a future causal curve crosses from the past side to the future side, and has at most one local parameter visit, by a spacelike slice chart and strict temporal-coordinate increase. Thus the set of surface visits in a compact parameter interval is closed and locally isolated, hence finite. If two visits existed choose consecutive ones $t_1<t_2$. The connected intervening image, which avoids the surface, must lie in one of $Q^-,Q^+$. Near $t_1$ it lies in $Q^+$, whereas near $t_2$ it lies in $Q^-$. This is impossible. Therefore there is exactly one visit.

facts.label: L5
facts.text: [L5] Quotient topology: for a surjection $\pi:Z\to Q$ with the quotient topology a subset $A\subseteq Q$ is open exactly when $\pi^{-1}(A)$ is open, and $\pi$ is continuous; a continuous injective open map is a homeomorphism onto its image ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]], [[def-continuity-real]]).

steps.claim: ($p_M$ and $p_{M'}$ are open injections.) For open $A\subseteq M$ the saturation is $$\pi^{-1}\bigl(p_M(A)\bigr)=\iota_M(A)\cup\iota_{M'}\bigl(\varphi(A\cap U)\bigr),$$ which is open in $Z=\iota_M(M)\sqcup\iota_{M'}(M')$ because $A$ and $A\cap U$ are open and $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism onto its image ([L2]); hence $p_M(A)$ is open in $Q$ ([L5]), and similarly for $p_{M'}$. If $p_M(p)=p_M(q)$ with $p\ne q$, then $\iota_M(p)\sim\iota_M(q)$ requires $\iota_M(p)=\iota_{M'}(\varphi(p))$ or $\iota_M(q)=\iota_{M'}(\varphi(q))$, impossible inside the disjoint union, or $\iota_M(p)=\iota_M(q)$, i.e. $p=q$; so $p_M$ is injective, and similarly $p_{M'}$. Both are continuous as compositions of the continuous inclusions with $\pi$ ([L5]).

(Smooth atlas.) Let $\{(V_i,\phi_i)\}_{i\in\mathbb N}$ and $\{(V'_k,\phi'_k)\}_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be countable atlases of $M$ and $M'$ ([L2]); their existence uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ applied to the countable bases of the two manifolds. Then $$\bigl\{(p_M(V_i),\;\phi_i\circ p_M^{-1})\bigr\}_{i\in\mathbb N}\cup\bigl\{(p_{M'}(V'_k),\;\phi'_k\circ p_{M'}^{-1})\bigr\}_{k\in\mathbb N}$$ is a countable open cover of $Q$ (step 3.1) by homeomorphisms onto open subsets of $\mathbb R^4$. Its transition maps are of the form $\phi_{i_0}^{-1}\circ\phi_{i_1}$, the primed analogue, or $\phi'_k\circ\varphi\circ\phi_i^{-1}$ (suitably restricted) on the overlap in $p_M(U)$; the first two are smooth because the atlases are smooth, and the third is smooth because $\varphi:(U,g|_U,\psi|_U)\to M'$ is a diffeomorphism onto the open set $\varphi(U)$ ([L2]). Hence $Q$ is a smooth four-manifold with this structure, and it is the unique structure making $p_M,p_{M'}$ diffeomorphisms onto their images, since any such structure has these charts in its atlas.

(Hausdorffness.) Two distinct classes represented in the same member are separated by images of disjoint open neighborhoods there, using step 2.1. For the remaining case choose representatives $z\in M\setminus U$ and $w\in M'\setminus\varphi(U)$. If $z
otin\overline U$, choose an open neighborhood $V
i z$ disjoint from $U$. Its image has no representative in $M'$, so is disjoint from the open full image $p_{M'}(M')$ containing $[w]$. The symmetric argument applies when $w
otin\overline{\varphi(U)}$. Otherwise $z\in\partial U$ and $w\in\partial\varphi(U)$. If every pair of their image neighborhoods met, then for every open $V
i z$, $V'
i w$ there would be $x\in V\cap U$ with $\varphi(x)\in V'$, by the exact overlap relation. This would be a corresponding boundary pair, contrary to [L1]. Thus the classes have disjoint neighborhoods.

For uniqueness, the sets $Q^\pm=p_M(I_M^\pm(\Sigma))\cup p_{M'}(I_{M'}^\pm(\Sigma'))$ are open and disjoint, and $Q=Q^-\sqcup\bar j(\Sigma)\sqcup Q^+$: this follows from the member side decompositions and their agreement on the common subdevelopment by causal convexity and future cone preservation. The surface is closed since its trace in each open member image is the closed member Cauchy surface. Near any surface point a future causal curve crosses from the past side to the future side, and has at most one local parameter visit, by a spacelike slice chart and strict temporal-coordinate increase. Thus the set of surface visits in a compact parameter interval is closed and locally isolated, hence finite. If two visits existed choose consecutive ones $t_1<t_2$. The connected intervening image, which avoids the surface, must lie in one of $Q^-,Q^+$. Near $t_1$ it lies in $Q^+$, whereas near $t_2$ it lies in $Q^-$. This is impossible. Therefore there is exactly one visit.

facts.label: L5
facts.text: [L5] Quotient topology: for a surjection $\pi:Z\to Q$ with the quotient topology a subset $A\subseteq Q$ is open exactly when $\pi^{-1}(A)$ is open, and $\pi$ is continuous; a continuous injective open map is a homeomorphism onto its image ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]], [[def-continuity-real]]).

steps.claim: ($p_M$ and $p_{M'}$ are open injections.) For open $A\subseteq M$ the saturation is $$\pi^{-1}\bigl(p_M(A)\bigr)=\iota_M(A)\cup\iota_{M'}\bigl(\varphi(A\cap U)\bigr),$$ which is open in $Z=\iota_M(M)\sqcup\iota_{M'}(M')$ because $A$ and $A\cap U$ are open and $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism onto its image ([L2]); hence $p_M(A)$ is open in $Q$ ([L5]), and similarly for $p_{M'}$. If $p_M(p)=p_M(q)$ with $p\ne q$, then $\iota_M(p)\sim\iota_M(q)$ requires $\iota_M(p)=\iota_{M'}(\varphi(p))$ or $\iota_M(q)=\iota_{M'}(\varphi(q))$, impossible inside the disjoint union, or $\iota_M(p)=\iota_M(q)$, i.e. $p=q$; so $p_M$ is injective, and similarly $p_{M'}$. Both are continuous as compositions of the continuous inclusions with $\pi$ ([L5]).

(Smooth atlas.) Let $\{(V_i,\phi_i)\}_{i\in\mathbb N}$ and $\{(V'_k,\phi'_k)\}_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be countable atlases of $M$ and $M'$ ([L2]); their existence uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ applied to the countable bases of the two manifolds. Then $$\bigl\{(p_M(V_i),\;\phi_i\circ p_M^{-1})\bigr\}_{i\in\mathbb N}\cup\bigl\{(p_{M'}(V'_k),\;\phi'_k\circ p_{M'}^{-1})\bigr\}_{k\in\mathbb N}$$ is a countable open cover of $Q$ (step 3.1) by homeomorphisms onto open subsets of $\mathbb R^4$. Its transition maps are of the form $\phi_{i_0}^{-1}\circ\phi_{i_1}$, the primed analogue, or $\phi'_k\circ\varphi\circ\phi_i^{-1}$ (suitably restricted) on the overlap in $p_M(U)$; the first two are smooth because the atlases are smooth, and the third is smooth because $\varphi:(U,g|_U,\psi|_U)\to M'$ is a diffeomorphism onto the open set $\varphi(U)$ ([L2]). Hence $Q$ is a smooth four-manifold with this structure, and it is the unique structure making $p_M,p_{M'}$ diffeomorphisms onto their images, since any such structure has these charts in its atlas.

(Hausdorffness.) Two distinct classes represented in the same member are separated by images of disjoint open neighborhoods there, using step 2.1. For the remaining case choose representatives $z\in M\setminus U$ and $w\in M'\setminus\varphi(U)$. If $z
otin\overline U$, choose an open neighborhood $V
i z$ disjoint from $U$. Its image has no representative in $M'$, so is disjoint from the open full image $p_{M'}(M')$ containing $[w]$. The symmetric argument applies when $w
otin\overline{\varphi(U)}$. Otherwise $z\in\partial U$ and $w\in\partial\varphi(U)$. If every pair of their image neighborhoods met, then for every open $V
i z$, $V'
i w$ there would be $x\in V\cap U$ with $\varphi(x)\in V'$, by the exact overlap relation. This would be a corresponding boundary pair, contrary to [L1]. Thus the classes have disjoint neighborhoods.

facts.label: L4
facts.text: [L4] Cauchy structure of the members and of $Q_0:=Q$: each $U_\alpha$ is a development of the data, hence globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $j_0(\Sigma)$; $\Sigma$ is acausal in each member and the side decomposition holds; a maximal connected portion of a curve that is inextendible in an ambient open set and enters an open subset is inextendible there; the push-up implications hold and every closed causal segment lies on an inextendible causal curve of the ambient manifold ([[thm-gr-cauchy-surface-implies-globally-hyperbolic]], [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a)5, [[lem-gr-cauchy-set-topology-and-graph]] clause (a), [[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (c)-(d), [[lem-gr-portion-inextendibility]], [[lem-gr-push-up-rule]], [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]).

steps.claim: (Canonical representation of an arbitrary development.) Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ be a development. By [L4] it is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $j(\Sigma)$. Let $X,\Phi,T$ be as in [L6]. Each integral curve is defined on $\mathbb R$ and satisfies $T(\Phi(t,y))=T(y)+t$, so it has no endpoint in $M$ and meets $j(\Sigma)$ exactly once. The map $\chi:\Sigma\times\mathbb R\to M$, $\chi(x,t)=\Phi(t,j(x))$, is therefore bijective and smooth. At $(x,t)$ its differential sends tangent vectors from $\Sigma$ to $d\Phi_t(dj(T_x\Sigma))$ and the time direction to $X_{\Phi(t,j(x))}=d\Phi_t(X_{j(x)})$. Since $j(\Sigma)$ is spacelike, $X_{j(x)}$ is not tangent to it; since $\Phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi_{-t}$, these images span $T_{\chi(x,t)}M$. Thus $\chi$ is a bijective local diffeomorphism, hence a diffeomorphism. Pulling back the metric, orientation representative and matter fields gives a tuple on $Z_0=\Sigma\times\mathbb R$ in $\mathcal X$, with $\chi\circ j_0=j$. This proves nonemptiness from the assumed development. The associated quotient embedding will be concluded after the quotient structure is established.

(Clause (d): the Cauchy property, at least one meeting.) Let $\gamma:\bar I\to Q$ be a causal curve inextendible in $Q$ and pick $t_0\in\bar I$ with $\gamma(t_0)\in Q_\alpha$. Let $J$ be the connected component of $\gamma^{-1}[Q_\alpha]$ containing $t_0$. By [L4] the restriction $\gamma|_J$ is inextendible in the open set $Q_\alpha$, so its pullback under the diffeomorphism $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is a causal curve in $U_\alpha$ inextendible in $U_\alpha$; by [L4] it meets $j_0(\Sigma)$ in exactly one parameter value, so $\gamma$ meets $\bar j(\Sigma)$.

(Compatible side decomposition.) In each member write $U_\alpha=I^-_\alpha(j_0\Sigma)\sqcup j_0\Sigma\sqcup I^+_\alpha(j_0\Sigma)$ as in [L4]. For $x\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ the side computed in $U_{\alpha\beta}$ is the same as in $U_\alpha$: a timelike curve inside the subdevelopment gives membership in the corresponding ambient side, and these sides are disjoint. The isometry $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ identifies these subdevelopment sides with those in its image in $U_\beta$, so the side in $U_\beta$ is identical. It follows that $Q^-:=\bigcup_\alpha\pi(I^-_\alpha(j_0\Sigma))$ and $Q^+:=\bigcup_\alpha\pi(I^+_\alpha(j_0\Sigma))$ are disjoint open sets and $Q=Q^-\sqcup S\sqcup Q^+$. In particular $S$ is closed. A future causal segment in a member that starts on its Cauchy surface lies, immediately afterwards, in its future side, and one ending on the surface lies immediately beforehand in its past side: extend the segment to an inextendible causal curve in that member; the unique Cauchy meeting and the disjoint side decomposition give the stated sides. More explicitly, any future-side point before the meeting would yield a timelike curve from the surface followed by a causal segment back to it, contrary to acausality; the past-side case after the meeting is its time reverse, using the push-up rule underlying the member side decomposition.

facts.label: L10
facts.text: [L10] Once $Q$ is second countable, its Hausdorff locally Euclidean smooth atlas makes it a smooth manifold, and Countable Choice gives a smooth partition of unity subordinate to its member cover. A finite positive weighted sum of vectors in one future timelike cone remains future timelike ([[def-smooth-manifold]], [[thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds]], [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

steps.claim: (A smooth global orientation representative.) The quotient is now a smooth manifold in the full sense of [L10]. Choose a subordinate locally finite smooth partition of unity $(\rho_\alpha)$ for the member cover and put $\bar N=\sum_\alpha\rho_\alpha(\pi|_{U_\alpha})_*N_\alpha$, extending each summand by zero outside $Q_\alpha$. Each summand is smooth because its support lies in $Q_\alpha$; the sum is locally finite. At every point the nonzero summands are positive multiples of vectors in the same future timelike component by step 4.1 and at least one coefficient is positive since the coefficients sum to one. Cone convexity makes $\bar N$ smooth, nowhere zero and future timelike. Every member map therefore preserves time orientation in the sense of preserving future cones. The metric and matter fields are the descended fields of step 4.1; the particular representative $\bar N$ is not claimed unique.

facts.label: L8
facts.text: [L8] Local exponential arguments are applied inside a member, which is a genuine second countable Lorentzian manifold: its joint exponential map has a smooth inverse near the diagonal, sufficiently small convex normal neighborhoods exist, and a contained timelike chord has timelike inverse velocity ([[lem-gr-joint-exponential-diffeomorphism]] clauses (a)-(c), [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]] clauses (a)-(b), [[lem-gr-convex-normal-causality]]). Uniqueness of the geodesic ODE lets these local maps patch in the quotient atlas; the maximal exponential domain on $Q$ is open and the exponential is locally smooth, as follows by following a compact geodesic segment through finitely many member charts ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]). This is a local construction, not an application of a theorem whose hypotheses already require second countability of $Q$.

steps.claim: (A countable dense set without assuming second countability of $Q$.) Choose a countable dense $D_0\subseteq S$. At every newly occurring point choose one tangent basis and retain it at all later stages; let $R_x$ be its rational span. Recursively set $D_{n+1}=D_n\cup\{\exp_xv:x\in D_n, v\in R_x, \bar g_x(v,v)<0, \exp_xv\text{ defined}\}$ and $D=\bigcup_nD_n$. These sets are countable by [L9], using the declared choice axioms for the recursion. To show density, take $p\in Q_\alpha$ and its member flow line from $z_0\in S$ to $p$ given by [L6]. If its flow parameter is zero, density of $D_0$ in $S$ suffices. Otherwise partition its compact segment into finitely many nonconstant timelike subsegments, each contained in a convex normal neighborhood within this member. Write their endpoints $z_0,\ldots,z_k=p$. For negative flow parameter the chords are past timelike; for positive parameter they are future timelike. We show inductively $z_i\in\overline{D\cap Q_\alpha}$: if $z_{i-1}$ has this property, choose $d\in D\cap Q_\alpha$ sufficiently near $z_{i-1}$. In the local two-point inverse the vector $v(d,z_i)$ is timelike by continuity and openness of the timelike set. Approximate it by a timelike $u\in R_d$ so closely that the member geodesic remains defined to time one and $\exp_du$ lies in any prescribed neighborhood of $z_i$ within $Q_\alpha$. Such $u$ exists by rational density and openness of the local exponential domain. If $d\in D_m$, then $\exp_du\in D_{m+1}\subseteq D$, with no claim that $m=i-1$. The exact inverse satisfies $\exp_d(v(d,z_i))=z_i$; no approximation error is added for this equality. This proves the induction and density of $D$ in $Q$.

(An explicit countable basis.) In each fixed tangent basis at $d\in D$, let $B_d(a,r)$ denote a Euclidean ball with rational center $a\in\mathbb Q^4$ and rational radius $r>0$. Form the family of all $\exp_d(B_d(a,r))$ for which the ball lies in the exponential domain and $\exp_d$ restricts to a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of $Q$. This family is countable by [L9] and consists of open sets by its definition. Given $p\in O$ with $O$ open, choose a member containing $p$ and use its joint exponential inverse near $(p,p)$. For all $d$ in a sufficiently small open neighborhood of $p$ in that member, there is a velocity $v(d,p)$ inside an open fiber domain $H_d$ on which $\exp_d$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open set containing $p$. Choose such $d\in D$ by step 5.1. The open set $H_d\cap\exp_d^{-1}(O)$ contains $v(d,p)$, so a rational translated ball in the fixed basis at $d$ contains $v(d,p)$ and lies in this open set. Its image is a family member containing $p$ and contained in $O$. This proves the basis criterion and hence second countability of $Q$.

facts.text: [L4] Cauchy structure of the members and of $Q_0:=Q$: each $U_\alpha$ is a development of the data, hence globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $j_0(\Sigma)$; $\Sigma$ is acausal in each member and the side decomposition holds; a maximal connected portion of a curve that is inextendible in an ambient open set and enters an open subset is inextendible there; the push-up implications hold and every closed causal segment lies on an inextendible causal curve of the ambient manifold ([[thm-gr-cauchy-surface-implies-globally-hyperbolic]], [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a)5, [[lem-gr-cauchy-set-topology-and-graph]] clause (a), [[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (c)-(d), [[lem-gr-portion-inextendibility]], [[lem-gr-push-up-rule]], [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]).

steps.claim: (Canonical representation of an arbitrary development.) Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ be a development. By [L4] it is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $j(\Sigma)$. Let $X,\Phi,T$ be as in [L6]. Each integral curve is defined on $\mathbb R$ and satisfies $T(\Phi(t,y))=T(y)+t$, so it has no endpoint in $M$ and meets $j(\Sigma)$ exactly once. The map $\chi:\Sigma\times\mathbb R\to M$, $\chi(x,t)=\Phi(t,j(x))$, is therefore bijective and smooth. At $(x,t)$ its differential sends tangent vectors from $\Sigma$ to $d\Phi_t(dj(T_x\Sigma))$ and the time direction to $X_{\Phi(t,j(x))}=d\Phi_t(X_{j(x)})$. Since $j(\Sigma)$ is spacelike, $X_{j(x)}$ is not tangent to it; since $\Phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi_{-t}$, these images span $T_{\chi(x,t)}M$. Thus $\chi$ is a bijective local diffeomorphism, hence a diffeomorphism. Pulling back the metric, orientation representative and matter fields gives a tuple on $Z_0=\Sigma\times\mathbb R$ in $\mathcal X$, with $\chi\circ j_0=j$. This proves nonemptiness from the assumed development. The associated quotient embedding will be concluded after the quotient structure is established.

(Clause (d): the Cauchy property, at least one meeting.) Let $\gamma:\bar I\to Q$ be a causal curve inextendible in $Q$ and pick $t_0\in\bar I$ with $\gamma(t_0)\in Q_\alpha$. Let $J$ be the connected component of $\gamma^{-1}[Q_\alpha]$ containing $t_0$. By [L4] the restriction $\gamma|_J$ is inextendible in the open set $Q_\alpha$, so its pullback under the diffeomorphism $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is a causal curve in $U_\alpha$ inextendible in $U_\alpha$; by [L4] it meets $j_0(\Sigma)$ in exactly one parameter value, so $\gamma$ meets $\bar j(\Sigma)$.

(Compatible side decomposition.) In each member write $U_\alpha=I^-_\alpha(j_0\Sigma)\sqcup j_0\Sigma\sqcup I^+_\alpha(j_0\Sigma)$ as in [L4]. For $x\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ the side computed in $U_{\alpha\beta}$ is the same as in $U_\alpha$: a timelike curve inside the subdevelopment gives membership in the corresponding ambient side, and these sides are disjoint. The isometry $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ identifies these subdevelopment sides with those in its image in $U_\beta$, so the side in $U_\beta$ is identical. It follows that $Q^-:=\bigcup_\alpha\pi(I^-_\alpha(j_0\Sigma))$ and $Q^+:=\bigcup_\alpha\pi(I^+_\alpha(j_0\Sigma))$ are disjoint open sets and $Q=Q^-\sqcup S\sqcup Q^+$. In particular $S$ is closed. A future causal segment in a member that starts on its Cauchy surface lies, immediately afterwards, in its future side, and one ending on the surface lies immediately beforehand in its past side: extend the segment to an inextendible causal curve in that member; the unique Cauchy meeting and the disjoint side decomposition give the stated sides. More explicitly, any future-side point before the meeting would yield a timelike curve from the surface followed by a causal segment back to it, contrary to acausality; the past-side case after the meeting is its time reverse, using the push-up rule underlying the member side decomposition.

steps.claim: (The set $D$.) Choose a countable dense subset $S_0\subseteq\bar j(\Sigma)$ ([L2]) and set $D_0:=S_0$. Recursively, given the countable set $D_n$, choose by Countable Choice a basis $(e_1(x),\dots,e_4(x))$ of $T_xQ$ at every newly added point, retaining all previously chosen bases, form $V_x^{\mathrm{rat}}$ as in the statement, and define $D_{n+1}$ by adding all points $\exp_x(v)$ with $x\in D_n$, $v\in V_x^{\mathrm{rat}}$ timelike and $\exp_x(v)$ defined. steps.claim: (Chains of timelike chords, including the past direction.) Fix $p\in Q$ and a member $Q_\alpha$ containing it. In that member the complete flow of [L5] joins a point $z_0\in S:=\bar j(\Sigma)$ to $p$ with a parameter $t_1\in\mathbb R$. If $t_1=0$, then $p\in S$ and is already in the closure of $D_0$. Otherwise finitely many convex normal neighborhoods cover this compact flow segment; a sufficiently fine finite partition of the segment has each subsegment contained in one of those neighborhoods. Write the ordered endpoints along the flow from $S$ to $p$ as $z_0,\ldots,z_k=p$. The inverse velocity $w_i=v(z_{i-1},z_i)$ for each contained joining geodesic is timelike by [L4], using future chords when $t_1>0$ and past chords when $t_1<0$ (reverse the future-directed chord and use the time reversal of the geodesic). The recursion includes both future and past timelike vectors.

facts.label: L3

facts.text: [L4] Timelike chords in convex balls: if $x\ll z$ are two points of a strictly convex normal ball $B$ and $z$ lies on the endpoint set in $B$ of a future timelike curve with image in $B$ starting at $x$, then $z=\exp_x(w)$ for a timelike $w$ ([[lem-gr-convex-normal-causality]] clause (a), applied with base point $x$). The set of timelike vectors at a point is open in the tangent space, and the rational span of a basis is dense in the tangent space in the coordinates of that basis ([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]).

steps.claim: (Chains of timelike chords, including the past direction.) Fix $p\in Q$ and a member $Q_\alpha$ containing it. In that member the complete flow of [L5] joins a point $z_0\in S:=\bar j(\Sigma)$ to $p$ with a parameter $t_1\in\mathbb R$. If $t_1=0$, then $p\in S$ and is already in the closure of $D_0$. Otherwise finitely many convex normal neighborhoods cover this compact flow segment; a sufficiently fine finite partition of the segment has each subsegment contained in one of those neighborhoods. Write the ordered endpoints along the flow from $S$ to $p$ as $z_0,\ldots,z_k=p$. The inverse velocity $w_i=v(z_{i-1},z_i)$ for each contained joining geodesic is timelike by [L4], using future chords when $t_1>0$ and past chords when $t_1<0$ (reverse the future-directed chord and use the time reversal of the geodesic). The recursion includes both future and past timelike vectors.

(Propagation of closure, without a stage-index assumption.) Work in $Q_\alpha$ and prove $z_i\in\overline{D\cap Q_\alpha}$ by induction. The case $i=0$ follows from the density of $D_0$ in $S$, since $S$ lies in every member. Suppose the claim holds for $z_{i-1}$, and prescribe any open neighborhood $O$ of $z_i$ within this member. The two-point inverse $v(q,z_i)$ is defined for $q$ close to $z_{i-1}$ in the convex neighborhood of step 1.2 and tends to the timelike vector $w_i$. Hence, for sufficiently close $q$, it is timelike. Choose such a $d\in D\cap Q_\alpha$ by the induction hypothesis. There is an open neighborhood of $v(d,z_i)$ in $T_dQ$ on which vectors remain timelike, the member geodesic remains defined to time one, and its exponential image lies in $O$, by openness and continuity of the member exponential. Choose a vector $u$ in the fixed rational span at $d$ in this neighborhood. Its quotient exponential equals its member exponential by uniqueness of the geodesic ODE and remains in $O$. As $d\in D_m$ for some $m$, the recursion gives $\exp_du\in D_{m+1}\subseteq D$. This proves that every such $O$ meets $D\cap Q_\alpha$, completing the induction. The exact inverse identity $\exp_d(v(d,z_i))=z_i$ has zero error; only approximation of this vector by $u$ contributes an endpoint error.

facts.label: L2
facts.text: [L2] Inside a member containing a prescribed point $p$, the joint exponential map $(q,v)\mapsto(q,\exp_qv)$ has a diffeomorphic restriction near $(p,0)$ with image containing a product neighborhood of $(p,p)$. Its smooth inverse gives $v(q,p)$ for every $q$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $p$. For each such $q$, its open fiber domain $H_q$ maps diffeomorphically onto an open subset of the member containing $p$ ([[lem-gr-joint-exponential-diffeomorphism]] clauses (a)-(c)). This argument can be performed entirely inside the member, even without using second countability of $Q$.

steps.claim: (The basis criterion.) Let $p\in O\subseteq Q$ with $O$ open. Choose a member containing $p$ and the product neighborhood of $(p,p)$ supplied by [L2]. Its first factor is an open neighborhood $V$ of $p$ in $Q$. Choose $d\in D\cap V$ by density. The inverse velocity $v(d,p)$ lies in $H_d$, where $\exp_d$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of this member. Thus $H_d\cap\exp_d^{-1}(O)$ is an open neighborhood of $v(d,p)$ in $T_dQ$. In the chosen basis at $d$, select a rational translated ball $B_d(a,r)$ containing $v(d,p)$ and contained in this neighborhood by [L3]. By [L1]-[L2], the quotient exponential on this ball agrees with the member exponential and restricts to a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of $Q$, so its image belongs to $\mathcal B$ and satisfies $p\in\exp_d(B_d(a,r))\subseteq O$.

facts.label: L1

facts.label: L5
facts.text: [L5] Connectedness of members and of $Q$: if $\Sigma$ is connected, every member $U_\alpha$ is connected, and $Q$ is connected. Indeed, each member contains $j_0(\Sigma)$ and is a development, so a maximal timelike geodesic through any point is inextendible in that member and meets its Cauchy surface. Its connected image lies in the component of that point, proving every component meets $j_0(\Sigma)$ ([[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clause (b), [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a)5); the member maps identify these initial surfaces, so the union $Q$ of the images is connected.

steps.claim: (Uniqueness.) Let $Q,Q'$ both be maximal developments of the data. By maximality of $Q'$ applied to the development $Q$, there is a data-fixing development embedding $\Phi:Q\to Q'$; by maximality of $Q$ applied to $Q'$, there is $\Phi':Q'\to Q$. The composition $\Phi'\circ\Phi:Q\to Q$ is a data-fixing isometric immersion of the development $Q$ into itself (compositions of isometric immersions preserving the data and the time orientation are again such); by [L4] it is the identity of $Q$ because $Q$ is connected by [L5]. Similarly $\Phi\circ\Phi'=\mathrm{id}_{Q'}$. Hence $\Phi$ is a data-fixing isometry with inverse $\Phi'$, and $Q,Q'$ are isometric over the data.

steps.claim: (Relating the postulates to the mathematical model.) By [F1] and [F2] the field law and matter equations are those of the specified fixed model, with its complete data and actual admissibility/local uniqueness obligations; the four concrete sectors of [[thm-gr-high-regularity-selected-matter-development]] are included at their stated branch hypotheses. By [A1] the constraint equations are the model's compatibility conditions on the data.

(Conditional character and scope.) The chain of steps 1.1-4.1 is a conditional deduction: each physical ingredient enters only through the adopted postulates [F1]-[F2], and each mathematical step is a theorem with explicitly stated hypotheses. The deduction establishes no statement about the physical universe and no observational claim; if a sector's regularity assumptions or the constraint equations fail for data of interest, the deduction does not apply. This completes the proof of the conditional assertion.

steps.claim: (The maximal development exists and is unique.) Applying [F4] with step 2.1 as the nonemptiness input, the data have a maximal development $(M_{\mathrm{max}},g_{\mathrm{max}},N_{\mathrm{max}},j_{\mathrm{max}},\psi_{\mathrm{max}})$ which is unique up to a unique data-fixing isometry, and every development embeds into it. This is (a) and (b).

(Global hyperbolicity.) By [F4] the maximal development is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $j_{\mathrm{max}}(\Sigma)$; hence the model's initial-value problem restricted to the constraint-satisfying data is deterministic: two iterations of the same data are isometric fixing the initial surface. This is (c).

steps.claim: ($\psi$ is a data-fixing isometry.) The translation $\psi$ is a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^{1,3}$ preserving $\eta$, the time orientation and (vacuously) the matter fields, and $\psi\circ j=j'$ by definition of $j,j'$. Hence $\psi:M\to M'$ is a development embedding of the whole of $M$, and $(M,\psi)$ is a common subdevelopment ([[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clauses (b)-(c), [[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]] clause (a)).

facts.label: L2
facts.text: [L2] Common subdevelopments and the maximal common development: $(M,\psi)$ is a common subdevelopment of $M$ and $M'$ ([[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]] clause (a)), the maximal one exists and contains every common subdevelopment with the same map ([[lem-gr-maximal-common-development]] clauses (a)-(b)), and the pair quotient of [[lem-gr-development-pair-gluing]] is a development of the data in which both members embed by data-fixing development embeddings.

In particular $U$ has no boundary in $M$, hence no corresponding boundary points, in accordance with [[lem-gr-no-corresponding-boundary-points]]. This is (a).

(The quotient.) By [[lem-gr-development-pair-gluing]] the quotient $Q:=(M\sqcup M')/{\sim}$ with the identifications along $\psi$ is a development of the data and the maps $p_M,p_{M'}$ are data-fixing development embeddings; here every point of $M$ is identified with its image in $M'$ and conversely, so the canonical map $M\to Q$, $p\mapsto[p]$, is a bijection and an isometry: its inverse is the map sending the class of $m\in M$ to $m$ and the class of $m'\in M'$ to $\psi^{-1}(m')$, which is well defined because $m'\sim\psi^{-1}(m')$ and because $\psi$ is a bijection. facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] Time separation: $\tau_q$ is finite on $J^-(q)$, the supremum of length over causal curves from a point $r$ to $q$ is attained exactly on causal geodesics, and in a causally convex normal neighbourhood of $q$ one has $\tau_q(r)=\sqrt{-g_q(\exp_q^{-1}r,\exp_q^{-1}r)}$ ([[lem-gr-time-separation-maximizers]] clauses (a)-(c)).

steps.claim: (The distance formula.) For $r\in J^-(q)$ the displacement $q-r=(\Delta t,\Delta x)$ is causal, and the unique maximizer of the Lorentzian length from $r$ to $q$ is the straight timelike segment, whose length is $\sqrt{(\Delta t)^2-|\Delta x|^2}=\sqrt{(t-1)^2-|x|^2}$ when the displacement is timelike; for lightlike displacement the value is $0$; this is the Minkowski instance of the attainability and geodesy of maximizers in [[lem-gr-time-separation-maximizers]] clause (a).

(At most one meeting along a causal curve.) facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] The dense-set recursion of [[lem-gr-development-quotient-dense-set]] with initial set $j(\Sigma)$ and datum $D_0=S_0$ produces the countable set $D$ of that lemma.

steps.claim: (One exponential step produces the rational points with nonzero time coordinate.) In the standard coordinates the exponential map is $\exp_d(v)=d+v$ ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]: geodesics are straight lines with affine parameter in flat coordinates). For $d=(0,q)\in\mathbb Q^3\times\{0\}=D_0$ and a rational vector $v=(a,w)\in\mathbb Q^4$ the point $d+v=(a,q+w)$ lies in $D_1$ whenever $v$ is timelike, i.e. $a^2>|w|^2$. Given $(a,b)\in\mathbb Q^4$ with $a\ne0$, choose $q:=b$ and $w:=0$; then $v=(a,0)$ satisfies $\eta(v,v)=-a^2<0$, so it is timelike, and $(a,b)\in D_1$. Every exponential step from a rational point using a rational vector remains rational, so induction gives $D\subseteq\mathbb Q^4$. Hence $\{r\in\mathbb Q^4:\ r^0\ne0\}\subseteq D_1$, and $D_0$ supplies the points with $r^0=0$, so $\mathbb Q^4\subseteq D$.

(Countability and density.) $D$ is countable by the construction ([[lem-gr-development-quotient-dense-set]], [[def-countable]]) and contains $\mathbb Q^4$, which is dense in $\mathbb R^{1,3}$ by the density of $\mathbb Q$ in $\mathbb R$ coordinatewise ([[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]); hence $D$ is dense and meets $j(\Sigma)=\{t=0\}$ in $\mathbb Q^3\times\{0\}$.

facts.label: L2
facts.text: [L2] The exponential family of rational balls is a countable basis of $Q$ ([[lem-gr-development-quotient-second-countable]]); the exponential map of Minkowski spacetime in standard coordinates is $v\mapsto d+v$ along straight geodesics ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (a)).

Since $d,a$ are rational, its centers are rational; conversely every rational center is obtained by taking $a=0$ and that center as $d$. Thus it is exactly the Euclidean rational-center family declared above.  For $d\in D$ and rational $r>0$ the set $\exp_d(B(0;r))=d+B(0;r)$ is the open Euclidean ball of radius $r$ around $d$ centred at a rational point with rational radius; the family of all such balls is a countable basis of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]], [[def-second-countable-space]]). In particular $\mathcal B$ as defined in the statement is a countable basis of the topology of $M$, so $M$ is second countable, in accordance with [[lem-gr-development-quotient-second-countable]].
